description: Composite group of two distinct images. The first is a pair of engineering drawings of test specimens: (a) a round tensile specimen with a 30 mm parallel gauge length, Ø5 mm gauge diameter, R5 shoulder fillets, M12 threaded grip ends, a 13 mm grip length and 60° end chamfers, overall length 65 mm; (b) a Charpy impact specimen 55 mm long with a 10 × 10 mm cross-section and a V-notch 2 mm deep. The second image is a mechanical-property plot, labelled (a), of engineering stress σE (MPa, 0-1500) versus engineering strain εE (%, 0-80) for Fe30Mn11AlxC(1050°C): curves for 0.6C (black), 1.0C (red), 1.2C (green), 1.5C (blue). Increasing C raises strength but lowers ductility — 1.5C peaks near 1200 MPa but fails earliest (around 22% strain), 1.2C plateaus near 1000 MPa and fails near 37%, while 0.6C and 1.0C are weaker but far more ductile, failing beyond 55-63% strain. Dashed arrows mark the fracture points from which the engineering fracture stress σEF is read. Together the panels define the specimen geometry and the tensile response.

subfigures.description: Engineering drawing of a round tensile specimen: 65 mm overall length, 30 mm parallel gauge section, Ø5 mm gauge diameter, R5 shoulder fillets, M12 threaded grip ends, 13 mm grip length, 1 mm shoulder step and 60° end chamfers (dimensions in mm).

Engineering drawing of a Charpy impact specimen: 55 mm long, 10 × 10 mm square cross-section, with a 2 mm deep V-notch drawn on the top face and a section view of the 10 × 10 mm end (dimensions in mm).
Engineering stress σE (MPa) vs engineering strain εE (%) plot for Fe30Mn11AlxC(1050°C) with four curves labelled 0.6C, 1.0C, 1.2C, 1.5C; dashed arrows mark each curve's fracture point.

observations.observation: The tensile-specimen drawing (a) is dimensioned in mm: 65 overall length, 30 gauge length, Ø5 gauge diameter, R5 fillet radius, 13 grip length, 1 mm shoulder step, M12 threads and 60° end chamfers.
The Charpy specimen drawing (b) is dimensioned in mm: 55 length, 10 × 10 cross-section, V-notch 2 mm deep.
The stress-strain plot axes are σE, Engineering stress, MPa (0 to 1500) against εE, Engineering strain, % (0 to 80).
The stress-strain legend reads Fe30Mn11AlxC(1050°C) with curves 0.6C (black), 1.0C (red), 1.2C (green) and 1.5C (blue).
The 1.5C (blue) curve reaches the highest peak stress, near the 1200 MPa gridline, and terminates earliest at low strain (around 22%).
The 0.6C and 1.0C curves are the lowest in stress but extend to the largest strains, failing beyond roughly 55-63%, i.e. increasing C raises strength but reduces ductility.
Dashed arrows are drawn at the end of each stress-strain curve, indicating the fracture points.
The caption states Fig. 1 gives the geometries of the tensile (a) and Charpy impact (b) specimens.
The citing text states the tensile specimens had a gauge length of 25 mm and diameter of 5 mm, which disagrees with the 30 mm gauge length dimension printed on drawing (a).
The citing text states tensile tests used an initial strain rate of 1.1 × 10^-3 s^-1 at ambient temperature on an MTS machine.
The citing text states Charpy specimens were cut with the V-notch perpendicular to the rod axis and tested on an MTS impact tester (500 J capacity) at -40 °C.
The citing text states the stress-strain jumps after yielding are caused by removal of the extensometer and do not affect property measurements.
The citing text states the arrows in the stress-strain figure illustrate determination of the engineering fracture stress σEF.
The citing text states samples were solution-treated at 1050-1100 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching, and that reported data are the average of two specimens.

unreadable_items: Conflict rather than illegibility: drawing (a) prints a 30 mm gauge length while the citing text states 25 mm.
